[$grill-with-docs](/Users/atbaker/Projects/atbaker/mcpkart/.agents/skills/grill-with-docs/SKILL.md) Okay - now let's start planning out a fresh evolution of this same concept. My goal for this project: create a fun, interesting way for developers to try and learn more about the latest LLM models, via a competitive kart racing game inspired by Mario Kart.\
\
The idea is that we implement a simplified version of Mario Kart, but all the players are AI agents which control their racers via an MCP Server we ship alongside the game. Human users connect to a race and optionally give their AI agent some racing strategy instructions (e.g. "be more cautious on turns" or "always use power ups as soon as you get them"). But then the race itself unfolds without end user input - instead the AI agents control the kart via the MCP Server: steering, acceleration, breaking, use a power up - maybe even a handbrake. The race should probably have 3 laps and end users can watch it via a web UI (or maybe via an MCP App / a Codex Plugin / a Claude Code "mod"? Not sure which approach is best). Users authenticate via a GitHub OAuth app, so their racer name is their GitHub username. Later on we might add the ability to be part of a racing "team" via the user's GitHub organizations. Users can join races via a lightweight matchmaking system to connect them with other live racers, or just race against bots / have live races get padded out with bots (I'm undecided if we should do 6 or 8 racers per race). For the "bot" racers, we just run those ourselves using maybe Pi or OpenCode or a similar OSS harness. We'll have public leaderboards which show the winningest racers and also, ideally, the winningest models and/or MCP clients (e.g. Claude Code vs. Codex).\
\
I work for Temporal and am doing this project for work, so we should also make it a showcase of how well Temporal works with AI agents and MCP. I'm thinking that could happen in a few ways: maybe the race itself is a Temporal Workflow (if we can get it to be performant enough to support a realtime race - might have to use local Activities or something). If that's not possible, then at least using Temporal to power most other parts of the platform should be sufficient: the MCP server, our orchestration for each race, the matchmaking, etc.\
\
When I tried building this back in December, the models were too slow. Where this project could get really interesting is if it can illuminate the pareto frontier between performance and intelligence. In theory, the winningest models will need to be sufficiently low latency and also sufficiently smart to outwit the other racers. In December, even the most lightweight models were still too slow to keep the racers on the race track. Even when I compromised on the vision and basically made it a turn-based race with one second ticks instead of a realtime race, it still didn't work. But today, with Jev, Clef, and this new generation of System One models, I think there's a chance this concept could be viable.\
\
When we get to prod, we'll want to deploy it on GCP using Temporal Serverless Workers. But to start, I really just want to try rearchitecting and rebuilding this concept here in my dev environment to see if it's even viable. Do Jev, Clef, and the new OpenAI Decisions API respond fast enough in order to sufficiently control a realtime kart racer?\
\
A few other topics on my mind as we get started:\
\- The previous implementation of this project used Python, which is my preferred stack. But I wonder if Rust might be better for powering the race itself, now that we're aiming to do it in realtime instead of via one-second ticks?\
  \- My guess is we might have a couple different production services anyway, so using different stacks for each isn't a huge deal. We could use Rust for running the game itself and Python and FastMCP for the MCP server\
\- The visuals in the previous evolution in December were a bit dry. If our racing game is really viable, I might be interested in aiming for a 3D low polygon art style for the game UI. But for now, let's just stick with a 2D SVG-based UI you implement yourself\
\- Which brings me to how human users will experience the UI: we can of course provide their AI agent a spectator URL as part of our MCP server responses and tell the user to open the link in their own browser. But ideally, the user would be able to watch the match inside their chat window for their AI agent of choice. MCP Apps in theory should help with this? But I know the spec is unevenly adopted. Maybe Codex and Claude Code have their own plugin APIs for this? We should research our options\
\- As for the game mechanics: in the previous tick-based system we descoped a lot of things that make a kart game interesting (like collisions). I'd rather start this new exploration with the assumption that we can support a realtime kart game experience and thus create a higher fidelity version of a kart game. It doesn't need to be nearly as fancy as bona fide Mario Kart. But I'd want it to have realtime gameplay, collisions between racers (so some real-ish physics), a few power ups, etc.\
\
Feel free to ask me lots of questions as you plan. Also feel free to run some experiments. You can use the Codex CLI with the OpenAI Decisions API to test things out as you go along. And use Exa for research tasks liberally. Document our plan as go along.

That makes the first question much sharper: can an OpenAI Decisions model drive a kart fast enough to race in real time? I’ll focus the PoC on that control loop and defer matchmaking, OAuth, and embedded spectator UI until we have evidence.

The [official OpenAI guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions) confirms an important distinction: Decisions returns choices or scores, rather than calling tools. We can test driving with a small adapter that turns a chosen control input into an MCP call. Its advertised speedup doesn’t establish driving viability; we need to measure how old each observation is when the resulting control reaches the kart.

*** Add File: /Users/atbaker/Projects/atbaker/mcpkart/GLOSSARY.md
+# MCP Kart
+
+MCP Kart is a competitive kart racing game in which AI drivers race autonomously while people watch and compare their performance.
+
+## Language
+
+**Racer**:
+A competitor entered in a race, with an identity used for standings and results.
+_Avoid_: Player when it could mean the human spectator.
+
+**Kart**:
+The vehicle a racer controls on the track.
+
+**Driver**:
+The AI agent controlling a racer's kart.
+_Avoid_: Model when referring to the whole agent.
+
+**Racing strategy**:
+Instructions supplied by a human to guide their driver's choices during a race.
+
+**Bot**:
+A racer whose driver is operated by the game service rather than a participating user.
+
+**Spectator**:
+A person watching a race as it unfolds.
+
+**Direct control**:
+Driving by selecting steering, throttle, and braking inputs rather than asking an automatic controller to perform a maneuver.
+
+**Realtime race**:
+A race that advances with elapsed time while drivers make decisions, including while a driver is waiting for its model.
+_Avoid_: Turn-based race, decision tick.
*** Add File: /Users/atbaker/Projects/atbaker/mcpkart/docs/plan.md
+# MCP Kart revival plan
+
+Updated October 18, 2026. Planning is in progress; realtime driving viability has not been measured.
+
+The first question is whether the OpenAI Decisions API can drive a kart in real time through MCP. The eventual product is a fun way for developers to experience the trade-off between model speed and intelligence by watching autonomous kart races.
+
+## Confirmed first milestone
+
+- A solo kart completes three laps of a winding track at a useful racing speed.
+- The driver chooses steering, throttle, and braking directly. There is no automatic lane keeping or racing-line follower.
+- Physics advances continuously in wall-clock time while model requests are in flight. The kart holds its last control input between decisions.
+- A thin Python driver converts Decisions choices into MCP control calls. Codex, Claude Code, and other general-purpose agent clients are evaluated later.
+- A scripted driver establishes that the same track and physics are driveable and provides a comparison for the model.
+- Development is local, with a 2D SVG spectator view. Traffic, collisions, and power-ups follow the solo milestone.
+
+These decisions were confirmed in the first interview round. [The realtime timing decision](adr/0001-racing-time-is-independent-of-model-responses.md) preserves the intended comparison between intelligence and latency.
+
+## What the first milestone establishes
+
+A successful result establishes solo driving with this model, driver, observation format, track, and local network conditions. Competitive racing, general-purpose agent clients, multiplayer capacity, and production latency each require additional experiments.
+
+## Proposed experiment sequence
+
+The following sequence is a proposal pending the remaining interview decisions.
+
+1. **Endpoint smoke test.** Confirm access to `POST /v1/decisions` with the documented model. Record the request shape, model, and failure modes without logging credentials.
+2. **Physics reference.** Establish continuous simulation, a winding track, and a scripted driver. Measure simulation scheduling separately from inference. Freeze track difficulty and handling before measuring the model.
+3. **Delay tolerance.** Inject controlled observation and action delays into the scripted driver. Determine which delays and jitter prevent it from maintaining control. This diagnoses sensitivity; it does not establish that a model will drive equally well.
+4. **Decision latency.** Measure realistic changing observations and a small fixed control menu using a reused connection. Report sample counts, warm and cold behavior, latency distributions, errors, rate limits, and input usage. Disable hidden retries for timing runs.
+5. **Closed-loop driving.** Run the Decisions driver through MCP while physics keeps advancing. Capture the observation, chosen action, when that action took effect, and a spectator replay. Compare completion and driving performance with the reference.
+6. **Failure diagnosis.** Compare the same driver with and without MCP overhead, different action grids, and different observation sizes. Keep direct transport runs separate from the MCP milestone. Distinguish latency failures from poor decisions, incomplete observations, or inadequate controls.
+
+The critical timing measure is **observation age when the action takes effect**, not time to first token. Capture observation time, request start, complete response, and action application using one monotonic clock wherever possible. Also measure simulation lateness so an overloaded Python loop cannot silently slow the game.
+
+Track completion, progress, off-track time, lap times, action age, rejected or late actions, errors, and cost. Include sample counts with percentiles; a small smoke test cannot characterize the latency tail.
+
+## Decisions API findings
+
+The [official guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions) documents a public beta using `gpt-6-luna` at `POST /v1/decisions`. It returns predicates, choices, or rubric scores rather than requesting tool calls. It advertises roughly ten times faster answers than Responses, without establishing an absolute latency suitable for racing.
+
+The proposed driver asks for one choice among explicit low-level control combinations and maps the answer to an MCP call. A joint choice keeps steering and acceleration decisions coupled. A score is a probability-weighted rubric result, not a generated steering angle. The [API reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/decisions/methods/create) permits 2–255 choices; an initial 15–27-choice grid would fit within that limit. The exact grid remains to be chosen.
+
+No inference measurements have been run. Credential inspection found no `OPENAI_API_KEY` in the process environment or either archived service env file. The installed Codex CLI is version 0.141.0, uses ChatGPT login, and exposes no Decisions subcommand. Selecting a model in Codex is not evidence that a request used the Decisions endpoint.
+
+## Temporal and language boundary
+
+Proposed: keep the first physics and inference timing loop independent of Temporal, then add Temporal orchestration and measure its effect. Python is the initial candidate because it is the preferred stack; benchmark simulation scheduling before deciding whether Rust is needed.
+
+For the platform, a Race Workflow could own admission, start, cancellation, completion, and results while a separate runtime executes continuous physics. A long-running Activity and an external race service are both candidates; recovery and interruption semantics need an explicit design.
+
+[Temporal's Local Activity guidance](https://docs.temporal.io/local-activity) and [design notes](https://docs.temporal.io/design-patterns/local-activities) describe execution inside Workflow Tasks, result markers, and responsiveness constraints. Local Activities do not by themselves establish that a Workflow can host a responsive realtime race. This is an architectural hypothesis to test after model driving viability, not a settled production design.
+
+## Open interview decisions
+
+The next round will resolve:
+
+- Whether the driver receives structured telemetry and track geometry, pixels, or both.
+- A measurable success threshold for completion rate and race pace.
+- Whether the first simulation is also Python, with Rust reserved for measured bottlenecks.
+- How to provide API-key access for bounded inference experiments.
+
+After those decisions, resolve the concrete observation and control contract, action timing and stale-input policy, track and vehicle parameters, trial count, and experiment budget. Approve the resulting experiment specification before implementation.
+
+## Later product scope
+
+The broader concept remains autonomous three-lap racing with kart collisions, several power-ups, live spectators, public matchmaking, and service-operated bots. GitHub OAuth supplies racer identities; organization-based teams may follow. Race size remains undecided between six and eight racers.
+
+Leaderboards should distinguish racer identity, model, and agent client or harness. Public self-reported entries and controlled model comparisons will need different evidence standards before they can support claims about the best model.
+
+Browser spectator links, MCP Apps, and client-specific integrations need a separate compatibility investigation. A low-poly 3D presentation is a possible later evolution. Jev and Clef remain future model candidates; they have not been investigated for this first Decisions experiment.
+
+Production is intended for GCP and Temporal Serverless Workers. Hosting, service boundaries, multiplayer recovery, authentication, and capacity planning follow the local viability evidence.

+# First experiment: realtime driving through MCP
+
+Status: scope agreed; concrete defaults awaiting shared-understanding confirmation. No inference results yet.
+
+Test whether OpenAI Decisions, Jev, and Clef can directly drive a solo kart around three laps of a winding track in real time. Use the same local Python simulation, observation content, control menu, MCP transport, and track for each model. Access all models through OpenRouter's Decisions endpoint.
+
+## Agreed scope
+
+- Continuous wall-clock racing with direct steering, throttle, and brake inputs. The game does not wait for a model, and the driver receives no automatic lane keeping or racing-line control.
+- Structured telemetry and upcoming track geometry, with a live 2D SVG spectator view.
+- One request in flight per driver. Apply its result and obtain the next observation immediately; faster models can act more frequently.
+- Recoverable off-road slowdown and ordered checkpoints; no automatic resets during a trial.
+- Python simulation and driver first. Measure before considering a Rust simulation.
+- Initial model set: `openai/gpt-6-luna-decisions`, `typesafe/jev-1.14`, and `cloudflare/clef`.
+- At least eight of ten runs complete three laps without resets, with median completed-run race time within twice the scripted reference.
+- A $10 total spending cap across the first paid batch, including smoke tests, warm-ups, latency tests, and driving trials.
+
+## Proposed concrete defaults
+
+### Simulation and track
+
+Run fixed-step physics at 60 Hz, paced against a monotonic wall clock. Rendering and model requests have separate schedules. Record simulation lateness and elapsed-time drift; a run that silently slows the world cannot establish realtime viability.
+
+Use a small 2D vehicle model with position, heading, velocity, acceleration, braking, steering response, and limited grip. Start with a winding closed track containing straights, broad bends, and at least one bend requiring reduced speed. Calibrate handling and track dimensions with the scripted driver before model trials, then freeze them. This first experiment omits kart-to-kart collisions, items, handbrake controls, and damage; the simulation boundary should permit adding them later.
+
+Grass reduces acceleration and speed but leaves steering under the driver's control. Count a lap only after the kart passes ordered checkpoints on the valid route. Off-road travel cannot skip the required course. A failed run can end, but cannot reset itself and claim completion.
+
+### Observations and controls
+
+Send a compact structured observation containing observation identity and racing time, kart position and heading, velocity, current controls, lap/checkpoint progress, nearby road boundaries, and a preview of upcoming track geometry. Use documented units and a consistent coordinate frame. Relative track position and geometry are observations; recommended steering, braking points, or a computed racing line are not provided.
+
+Include fixed handling limits, the action definitions, and the same basic racing objective for every model. Begin with no growing conversation history or model-specific prompt tuning. Keep state comfortably below the selected provider's effective input limit and verify that geometry is not truncated.
+
+Start with 15 allowed actions: five normalized steering positions (`-1`, `-0.5`, `0`, `0.5`, `1`) combined with acceleration, coasting, or braking. Acceleration sets throttle to one and brake to zero; coasting sets both to zero; braking sets throttle to zero and brake to one. Steering positions map to fixed physical steering values. The selected action persists until replaced; the adapter adds no driving policy.
+
+Use one named `choice` question with all 15 joint actions as its criteria. Verify the exact request and response schema with OpenRouter. Provider scores or probability mixtures are not blended into an additional control policy in this experiment.
+
+### MCP and action timing
+
+Use a local MCP server with structured observations and control submission. The decisive driving runs use a real MCP client/transport rather than direct calls to simulation functions. A control response may include the next observation to avoid a redundant round trip, provided that behavior is identical across models.
+
+Attach observation and command sequence identities to controls. Apply accepted inputs at a defined physics-step boundary, record when they actually took effect, and reject duplicate or out-of-order commands. Acknowledging a queued command does not mean it has already affected physics.
+
+Model requests do not block physics. On a request error, refusal, invalid action, or missing reply, retain the last applied controls and record the event. Do not silently retry a timed decision, pause the world, automatically brake, or invoke a fallback driver. Cancellation closes the trial so a late reply cannot affect a subsequent race.
+
+The proposed trial deadline is three times that trial's scripted reference duration. An unfinished trial is recorded as a failure at the deadline. A network failure is part of the observed model/route result; a simulation scheduling failure is reported separately and cannot count as a passing trial.
+
+### Providers and spending
+
+Discover current provider endpoints and prices, choose and record a route for each model, and pin it for comparison with automatic fallbacks disabled. Select routes before collecting the comparison results; do not choose a different route in response to a losing race. Record the actual returned model and provider. These are model-plus-route comparisons through OpenRouter, rather than measurements of isolated inference compute.
+
+Load `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` from the local environment or ignored `.env`. Keep credentials out of logs and replays. Stop before the next request would exceed the $10 allowance, using a conservative allowance for in-flight work and a maximum request/token count as well as reported spending. If the cap stops a batch before ten trials per model, report the smaller sample as incomplete rather than changing the pass rule.
+
+## Experiment sequence
+
+1. **Offline reference:** verify direct control, lap/checkpoint correctness, off-road recovery, deterministic replay from recorded inputs, and reliable realtime simulation. The scripted driver uses the same action menu. It is a reference driver, never a rescue controller for the model.
+2. **Delay tolerance:** delay the reference driver's observations/actions by controlled amounts and add jitter. This measures the track's control sensitivity and helps interpret later failures.
+3. **Endpoint and latency tests:** verify each pinned route with a small smoke test, then measure changing realistic observations over reused connections. Separate cold and warmed requests and retain all errors. Use sample counts appropriate to the latency claims; do not infer a reliable p99 from a small pilot.
+4. **Driving screen:** run each model on the same track through MCP. Confirm that observation formatting, action mapping, and timing instrumentation work before committing the remaining budget to a batch.
+5. **Ten paired trials per model:** reuse ten predefined starting-condition seeds for every model and interleave model order to reduce time-of-day bias. Run trials sequentially initially so local concurrency does not confound the comparison. Freeze track, handling, prompts, and control menu for the batch.
+6. **Diagnose failures:** if needed, compare transport overhead, observation size, or control resolution as separately labeled experiments. Keep the original comparison results; changes require a new experiment configuration.
+
+## Evidence and interpretation
+
+For each request, record observation capture, request start, complete response, and action application times. Compute observation age at application, plus API round-trip time and MCP/control-queue time. Record physics lateness independently.
+
+For each trial, save configuration, seed, track/handling version, model/provider identity, observations and actions, completion, lap times, checkpoint progress, off-road time, errors, token usage, cost, and a replay. The SVG viewer shows the track, kart, progress, current controls, and whether the driver is waiting for a reply.
+
+Report completion out of all ten trials, median completed-run duration relative to the paired reference, off-road time, action-age distributions, errors, and cost. Preserve failures in the completion denominator. Show sample counts and mark any interrupted batch as incomplete. Passing on one track establishes a local solo-driving result; it does not establish collision handling, multiplayer capacity, embedded client compatibility, or universal model superiority.
+
+## Following milestones
+
+If solo driving works, add a competing kart and collisions, then power-ups and six/eight-driver load tests. Separately add Temporal race lifecycle orchestration and measure its overhead and recovery behavior. General-purpose agent clients, OAuth, matchmaking, leaderboards, embedded spectator UI, production hosting, and 3D presentation follow that evidence.
+

+
+- [Project plan](../plan.md)
+- [Verified API and model research](../research/decision-models.md)
+- [Racing time decision](../adr/0001-racing-time-is-independent-of-model-responses.md)

+
+The first rescued driving screen did not complete three laps with any of the three routes. Jev and Clef reached only 12 of 120 required checkpoints, despite travelling around the circuit repeatedly. These are exploratory single runs, not ten-run model rankings.
+
+An audit found no steering-sign or coordinate-transform bug. Jev selected acceleration for all 337 on-road decisions and never braked while on-road. It entered a roughly 20 m radius bend at 24 m/s. Luna sometimes turned away from the nearby road even when the heading and offset implied the opposite correction.
+
+The original observation requires converting radians and curvature into intuitive bend shape while distinguishing kart-relative geometry from road-relative geometry. Its nine samples can also miss narrow curvature peaks: a 3.8 m radius right bend around road position 87.9 m can fall between preview samples. +
+## Candidate representations
+
+| Profile | Evidence |
+| --- | --- |
+| `raw` | Existing world position/heading, signed offset and heading error in radians, nine ego-frame centreline points and curvature values, handling, checkpoint and rescue state. |
+| `road` | Explicit left/right offset and edge clearances; road/kart alignment in degrees; ego-frame velocity; preview tangent change from the current road tangent; bend direction and radius; dense summaries of the next three bend regions. |
+| `road_text` | The same road facts as `road`, expressed as a compact prose report inside structured state. |
+| `road_physics` | `road` plus the lateral acceleration required at the current speed, its ratio to current surface grip, and the grip-limited minimum steady turn radius. |
